Official answer A checked; editorial worked explanation:

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
Two waves X and Y are emitted simultaneously and each travels 300 km to a detector. Both have frequency 5.0 Hz. Their wavelengths in their respective media are 1100 m and 660 m. Using travel time=distance/speed, what is their arrival-time difference and which arrives first?

A. 55 s; X first
B. 36 s; X first
C. 55 s; Y first
D. 36 s; Y first

answer.text: B. vX=5×1100=5500 m s⁻¹ and vY=5×660=3300 m s⁻¹. Their travel times are 54.55 s and 90.91 s, a difference 36.36 s; X arrives first.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
At one instant, the electric-field vector in an electromagnetic wave points upwards in the page. Which pair gives possible directions for wave propagation and the magnetic-field vector?

A. Propagation right; magnetic field right
B. Propagation right; magnetic field out of the page
C. Propagation up; magnetic field left
D. Propagation up; magnetic field out of the page

answer.text: B. In an electromagnetic wave the electric field, magnetic field and propagation direction are mutually perpendicular. Only B satisfies that requirement.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A microphone beside a student records a clap and its echo from a wall. The students repeat the measurement at different wall distances. Explain why distances of 0.2 m and 30 m may be unsuitable.

answer.text: At 0.2 m the echo returns so soon that it may overlap the original clap or be difficult to resolve. At 30 m the returning sound may be too weak relative to background noise to identify its arrival accurately.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Students use a microphone to measure the delay between a clap and its echo from a wall. Describe one condition of the experimental surroundings that helps them identify the echo accurately.

answer.text: Use a quiet space with little background sound, so the echo pulse can be distinguished clearly in the recording. An alternative is a space without nearby competing reflecting surfaces, to avoid overlapping echoes.

evidence.review: Derived independently from the question and checked against the first-assessment2025 IB Physics guide; handwritten annotations are not answer evidence.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: In an echo experiment, distance d is measured from a microphone to a wall. A student claps close to the microphone, and the recorded delay t is measured from arrival of the direct clap to arrival of its echo. The graph shows t against d. (a) Identify evidence of a systematic error. (b) Suggest a plausible cause consistent with the sign of the offset.

answer.text: (a) The best-fit line does not pass through the origin: it reaches t=0 at a positive distance of about 0.4 m. Ideally t=2d/c for a source at the microphone. (b) The clap may be produced closer to the wall than the microphone. If it is ahead by x along the wall direction, the echo path is 2d−x while the direct path to the microphone is x, so t=2(d−x)/c and the distance intercept is+x. The graph alone does not uniquely establish the cause.

evidence.review: Derived independently from the question and checked against the first-assessment2025 IB Physics guide; handwritten annotations are not answer evidence.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A microphone records the delay t between a clap and its echo from a wall at distance d. Use the gradient of the fitted t-against-d graph to determine the speed of sound. A constant timing or distance offset may be present.

answer.text: The round-trip relation gives gradient m=Δt/Δd=2/c. Widely separated points on the fitted line are approximately(0.4 m,0 s) and(10 m,0.066 s). Thus m≈0.066/9.6=6.9×10⁻³ s m⁻¹ and c=2/m≈2.9×10² m s⁻¹. Small variations from reading the graph are reasonable.

answer.text:
Official answer D checked; editorial worked explanation:

For a point wave source, I is proportional to Y^2/x^2. Let the new amplitude be Y prime. Then 2 = (Y prime/Y)^2 (x/(x/2))^2 = 4(Y prime/Y)^2, so Y prime/Y = 1/sqrt(2). Thus Y prime = sqrt(2)Y/2. Therefore D.

evidence.detail: Official key page 3 gives D; explanation independently authored and checked.

parts.given_text: Editorial adaptation: use the supplied point-source model I proportional to Y²/r², where Y is the source amplitude and r is the distance from the source. The proportionality constant is unchanged between the two observations.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: (i) State what is meant by a transverse wave. The source graph shows displacement y against distance x for a wave on a string. (iii) The wave speed is 62 m s⁻¹. Use the graph to calculate the period to the correct number of significant figures.

answer.text: Official markscheme results; editorial worked explanation: (i) In a transverse wave, the displacement of the medium is perpendicular to the direction of propagation and energy transfer. (iii) Consecutive crests on the graph are separated by λ=1.20 m. Since v=λ/T, T=λ/v=1.20/62=1.93548×10⁻² s, which to two significant figures is 1.9×10⁻² s.

original-ib26mb1a-mcq-19:whole.hint: Use each wave’s own wavelength to find its speed. Calculate both journey times over the same distance before subtracting.
notes: Waves with the same frequency need not have the same speed when they travel through different materials.
Convert 300 km to 300000 m before dividing by speeds in metres per second; subtract the shorter time from the longer.

original-ib26mc1a-mcq-18:whole.hint: Check that the propagation direction is perpendicular to each field, as well as that the two fields are perpendicular.
notes: Electromagnetic waves are transverse: neither field oscillates parallel to the direction of travel.
A magnetic field perpendicular to the electric field is necessary but not sufficient; it must also be perpendicular to the propagation direction.

original-ib26mb1b-written-2-a:whole.hint: Consider separately whether the echo is distinguishable in time and whether its signal remains strong enough to detect.
notes: The echo makes an outward and return journey. Small distance means a very short delay; a longer distance improves separation but reduces the received signal.
Suitability depends on the pulse duration, equipment and surroundings. Give a physical measurement limitation for each distance rather than claiming that sound cannot travel that far.

original-ib26mb1b-written-2-b:whole.hint: Think about other sound signals that could obscure or be confused with the wall’s echo.
notes: Name a specific condition and connect it to the measurement. Quiet surroundings improve the signal-to-noise ratio.
Repeated trials reduce random variation, but cannot reliably recover a pulse that is consistently hidden among competing sounds.

original-ib26mb1b-written-2-ci-cii:whole.hint: Extrapolate the fitted line to zero delay, then check whether the assumed sound source really coincides with the measured distance reference.
notes: A constant offset shifts the fitted line away from the expected origin. Random scatter is a different feature and is not evidence of a fixed offset by itself.

The timer starts when the direct sound reaches the microphone. Account for that initial travel time as well as the reflected path; merely saying human reaction time is not appropriate for this recorded-signal method.

original-ib26mb1b-written-2-d:whole.hint: Relate a change in wall distance to the change in the complete outward-and-return travel time. Use differences between two fitted-line points.
notes: The graph plots time vertically, so its gradient has units s m⁻¹. Taking 2 divided by that gradient gives a speed in m s⁻¹.
A constant offset changes the intercept but not the gradient. Do not calculate 2d/t from a single point or replace the experimental result by a memorised room-temperature sound speed.

fast-ib-production-001-a-may-q17:whole.hint: Form a ratio using intensity proportional to amplitude squared divided by distance squared.
notes: Halving distance alone multiplies intensity by four, so the amplitude must decrease to give only a factor of two.
Take the positive square root because amplitude is a non-negative magnitude.

fast-ib-16794b5512ac31d3-3-wave:whole.hint: Use the direction of particle displacement relative to propagation for the definition, then read one full crest-to-crest wavelength from the graph.
notes: A transverse wave transfers energy along the string while elements of the string move perpendicular to that direction.
Measure wavelength between points in the same phase, such as adjacent crests, rather than from a crest to a trough.

fep-59e9fdff25044e14-q19:whole.text: B. In a quarter of a period the right-moving profile advances by λ/4. Translate the whole curve that distance to the right, keeping its amplitude and wavelength unchanged; this gives the profile in B.
